chapter: Wider talk: bands, places and players
title: Casino Gardens, Jack Tilson's band and Izzy Freeman
summary: He recalls the Casino Gardens, Tilson's band personnel, and Izzy Freeman.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs

blocks.x: Mm-hmm. And the casino gardens, I, I don't know what that was. Was that a beer garden or a restaurant or? Well, it was a...

A light club, a camaraderie? I, I, I, now wait a while. I'm trying to figure out what, what it, what it actually was. It was a, uh, I don't know, like, it was, well, anyway, I showed you the picture of things. Mm-hmm. But it was a, a big, uh, building, and, and it was a restaurant or a place where, where they had a stage, and, uh, it could have been a dance hall at one time.

Or it could have been a, a gathering of a lodge. You understand? Yeah, I see. That would have a dinner, or any kind of a seminar, or whatever you want to call those things, that, uh, somebody wanted to speak, uh, at the time, you know. But that, that, that's the, that's the place where the Wolverines played for a while, see. Mm-hmm. And then later on, Jack Tilson got the band, and Jack Tilson was, he was a promoter, see, politician guy. And later on, he became one of the councilmen in, in Annapolis. Mm-hmm. But he was, uh, uh, an MC, and, and did some vocalizing, see. He played drums, and he played pretty good drums, you know what I mean? But then when we, we got there and joined him the first time with the four men from Chicago, we had, we, we had Herb Wedman on piano of his band, and Skinny Bud played tenor, and, and, uh, and, I see who else was, oh, George Combs on banjo. Yeah. And we didn't have any bass at that time, see. Mm-hmm. And then, well, the second time we went back there, he, he was a politician, and he wasn't, what's the matter, it's a different thing. But, um, the second time, when Izzy Freeman would, uh, played for, for alto was, and later on, Izzy Freeman would play, kind of, with Paul White in his band, too.

Now, the last time I saw Izzy, he was a, uh, uh, recording manager for Columbia Studios out there in California. Oh, really? He worked in the studios out there, and, he was, he was a legitimate man, see. But, uh, he tried to, I mean, he wasn't the greatest, the greatest style as far as I'm starting. No. I mean, he played, played a lot of good clarinet, and, and, he, he, he, at that time, when he played with us, he, he was copying, uh, I don't know, whether, who, who, who was a great clarinet player at that time, you know. But, uh, he, he tried to play like, like Rapola, but he had a different kind of a tone on his horn, see. Mm-hmm. He didn't, didn't have the right kind of feeling to it. Not that he wasn't a good musician, he could read anything, and make arrangements and everything, you know. Yeah. But that, that was his part of the business, he was a legitimate man.
